1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6.name: Philidor Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6.background: Ruy López already recommended 2...d6 in his 1561 book, because 2...Nc6 allows the Ruy Lopez 3.Bb5, and the eighteenth-century master Philidor favoured it as an alternative to 2...Nc6. By the First World War it had almost completely vanished from top-level chess.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4.name: Philidor Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4.strategy: White strikes at once, attacking e5 a second time and threatening to open the centre. Black cannot simply recapture with the d-pawn, because queens would come off and the king would lose the right to castle, so Black has to choose how to meet the pressure while White keeps space and the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4.name: Philidor Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop to its most active square, aiming at f7, and leaves the central break for later. It is less forcing than striking in the centre at once, so Black gets time to finish development, but the solid, slightly passive structure stays and White sets the pace.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Nc3.strategy: Guards e4 with a developing move and keeps the central break in reserve. It is sound and flexible, but it leaves e5 unchallenged, so Black is not pushed to decide anything yet and gets time to reach a comfortable set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4 Be7.name: Philidor Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4 Be7.strategy: The natural, solid reply: the d6 pawn has shut in the bishop's diagonal, and e7 is the one good square it has. It guards f6 and g5, keeps the king's side tight and prepares castling. Black stays compact and passive, waiting for White to commit.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4 f5.name: Philidor Defence: Lopez Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4 f5.background: Already analysed in the Göttingen manuscript and played by Ruy López in 1575.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4 f5.strategy: Counterattacks e4 with a flank pawn, but it loosens the king's side and the diagonal to the king. White answers in the centre: if Black takes on e4 and recaptures the knight that takes e5, a queen check on h5 and then Qxe5+ wins the rook on h8.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4 Nc6.strategy: Defends e5 a second time with a developing move, so the centre is safe and development is natural. The cost is that the knight blocks the c-pawn and the d6 pawn still hems in the dark-squared bishop, so White can take more space in the centre and Black stays a little passive.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.c3.name: Philidor Defence: Steinitz Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.c3.background: Named after a game that Wilhelm Steinitz played against George MacDonnell.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.c3.strategy: Quiet and solid: it prepares a slow build-up with the d-pawn behind the bishop instead of forcing matters in the centre. The game stays closed and manoeuvring, and White can take its time because Black's set-up is solid but passive.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.d4.strategy: Strikes at e5 at once, with the bishop already aiming at f7. After the exchange in the centre White has open lines, a lead in space and a free development, while Black stays compact but passive behind the d6 pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.O-O.strategy: Castles first and keeps the central break for later. The king is safe and no weakness is created; White keeps the choice between a slow build-up and the break in the centre, at the price of giving Black a quiet tempo to finish development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4.name: Philidor Defence: Exchange Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4.strategy: The main line: Black resolves the tension at once instead of defending the pawn, which removes White's threat against e5. White gets the centre and a lead in space, while Black gets a compact position with few weaknesses and plays for a long, solid defence.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7.name: Philidor Defence: Hanham Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7.background: Named after the American master James Hanham, who played it eleven times at the 6th American Chess Congress in 1889; John Lord had played it twice at the 1868 British Chess Association Congress.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7.strategy: Keeps the tension and defends e5 a second time, aiming for a strongpoint defence of the pawn. The knight takes a modest square and blocks the c8-bishop, and f7 becomes a target; Black hopes to hold the centre and catch up in development later.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6.name: Philidor Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6.background: Tony Kosten attributes the move to Aron Nimzowitsch, who favoured it to avoid the line 3...Nd7 4.Bc4.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6.strategy: Counterattacks e4 instead of defending e5, and avoids the awkward bishop attack on f7 that Black faces after ...Nd7. White can take on e5 and bring the queen to d5 with the better chances, so Black must be ready for a slightly worse, simplified game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Bg4.strategy: Pins the knight against the queen, but the pin is hollow and the bishop does not defend e5. After White takes on e5 and Black recaptures with the d-pawn, queens come off, the knight is free to take e5 and Black has lost a pawn and the right to castle.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5.name: Philidor Defence: Philidor Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5.background: Philidor's own recommendation, and played several times by Paul Morphy in 1858. Bronstein, Mestel, Kosten and Nakamura have also played it, and leading authorities have dismissed it many times while it keeps returning.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5.strategy: The most aggressive reply: a flank pawn strikes at e4 and the centre. It loosens the king's side and the diagonal to the king, so White gets lasting attacking chances. Tricky if White is unprepared, but judged too risky and dubious.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Bd7.name: Philidor Defence: Philidor Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Bd7.strategy: Offers the e5 pawn without a plan. If White takes and Black recaptures, the bishop on d7 blocks the queen so no queens come off, but the knight simply takes e5, attacks the bishop and wins a pawn. Black gets nothing concrete for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Bg4 4.dxe5.strategy: Takes the pawn at once, and the pin on the knight is hollow: if Black recaptures with the d-pawn, queens come off, the knight is free to take on e5 and White wins a clean pawn while Black loses the right to castle.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Be2.strategy: Puts the bishop behind the knight, so the pin on the queen is gone and ...Bxf3 wins no time. It develops and prepares castling, but it lets Black take on d4 and trade bishops, which leaves a quiet, level-looking game instead of the pawn White could win.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Bg4 4.h3.strategy: Puts the question to the bishop at once: if it takes on f3, White recaptures with the queen and keeps the bishop pair; if it retreats, the capture on e5 is still there. It is sound but spends a tempo that the direct capture does not need.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Bg4 4.dxe5 Nd7.name: Philidor Defence: Albin-Blackburne Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Bg4 4.dxe5 Nd7.strategy: The best try after 3...Bg4: Black gambits the pawn and develops with tempo, aiming for three black pieces out against one white piece once the pawns are taken. Black plays for open lines and a lead in development; White must consolidate with care to keep the extra pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Bg4 4.dxe5 Bxf3.strategy: Trades the bishop for the knight and wins the pawn back next move, but White recaptures with the queen, keeps the bishop pair and develops the bishop to c4 with a strong attack on f7. Black is simply behind in development with nothing in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Bg4 4.dxe5 dxe5.strategy: Recaptures and allows the queen swap: after Qxd8+ Kxd8 the knight takes on e5 and attacks the bishop on g4, so White wins a clean pawn while Black has lost the right to castle.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4.name: Philidor Defence: Exchange Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4.strategy: The natural recapture: the knight lands on a strong central square, and White keeps a lead in space and development against Black's solid but passive camp. Nothing is hanging; White simply builds on a small, lasting edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3.name: Philidor Defence: Bird Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.c3.strategy: An offbeat gambit: White leaves the d4 pawn alone and offers a second pawn after it is taken, aiming for a lead in development and open lines. Black can simply accept, and White has to show that the pawns are worth it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4.strategy: The queen recaptures and keeps the centre, but she stands in the open and Black develops with tempo by attacking her. White gets central control only at the cost of time; playable, but less accurate than recapturing with the knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4.name: Philidor Defence: Morphy Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4.strategy: Declines to recapture and develops with pressure on f7, offering a pawn for speed. Black need not fear it: giving the pawn back and finishing development calmly is the safe answer, while greed and slow moves can be punished.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.name: Philidor Defence: Exchange Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.strategy: The main move: it develops with a tempo on the e4 pawn, so White has to defend it. Black then follows with a compact, solid set-up and early castling, giving up some space but leaving no weaknesses to attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 g6.name: Philidor Defence: Larsen Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 g6.background: Bent Larsen tried the move in a few games, including a draw against Mikhail Tal in 1969.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop for pressure on the long diagonal. Flexible, but slow: Black spends time on the bishop while White's centralised knight and quicker development give White more space, so Black is a little behind.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once, but White simply takes: after ...Qxd5 the queen faces a check on the e-file or an attack from Nc3, and Black falls behind in development. A rare try that hands White an easy lead.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 d5 5.e.name: Philidor Defence: Paulsen Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 d5 5.e.background: Named the Paulsen Attack after Louis Paulsen; Black's 4...d5, which allows it, is a rarely seen alternative.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 d5 5.e.strategy: Takes the pawn and opens the e-file against a king that is still in the centre. If the queen recaptures, White gains time with a check on the e-file and by attacking her with a knight, and so keeps the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 d5 5.N.strategy: Develops with a threat to the d5 pawn and keeps the central knight, but it allows Black to take on e4 and relieve the centre. White gets active pieces and a small lead in development without the pressure on the e-file that taking the pawn gives.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 d5 5.e.strategy: Shuts the e-file instead of opening it, and so throws away White's edge. The pawn on e5 has no defender, and ...Bc5 attacks the knight at once, so Black's pieces come out with tempo and Black equalises easily.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Defends the attacked e4 pawn with a developing move, the obvious answer. White keeps the knight on d4 in the centre and every piece works together, so Black has to develop carefully against the lead in space.
Defends e4 with the bishop and keeps the knight in the centre. The bishop blocks the queen's own file, so White develops without a clear plan, and Black can finish development comfortably.

Gains a tempo with check, but the bishop is easily traded off on d7, and the exchange eases Black's development. White keeps only a small space edge, and e4 still needs a defender once the bishops are gone.

The bishop's natural square and the first step to castling. Black stays compact: a pawn move such as ...c5 would weaken d6, so development and a safe king come first, and Black accepts that White has more space.

Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and keep the king safe behind it. Black is solid, but the set-up is slower in the centre than quick development, and White gets time to build an active position and a space advantage.

Develops a piece and challenges the central knight. If White exchanges, Black gets doubled c-pawns and the half-open b-file; the move is playable but loosens the compact structure that makes this defence safe.
Hits the knight with a tempo but weakens d6 before Black has castled. If Black blocks the bishop check on b5 with the bishop, the queen loses its grip on d6 and a knight jump to f5 wins the pawn.

A quiet, flexible development: the bishop heads for castling and keeps White's options open instead of rushing an attack. It is a respected alternative to the more active bishop moves, and White keeps a small space advantage.

Points the bishop at the d6 pawn and prepares to put the queen on d2 and castle long. White keeps a small but lasting space advantage, while Black has to castle and find a way to free the position without weakening d6.

Fianchettoes the bishop to bear on the centre and the long diagonal while the knight keeps e4 guarded. It is a slower, strategic set-up with the king safe on the short side, and Black gets time to break in the centre.

Aims the bishop at f7, but it stands exposed to Black's central counter: after castling Black can take on e4 and play ...d5, hitting the knight and the bishop together and regaining the piece. White gets an active bishop and little lasting.

Black's intended set-up: the king is safe and the structure compact, with no weaknesses to attack. White keeps a small space edge, but Black has a solid position and can strike back in the centre later.

Develops the knight with a challenge to d4. If White exchanges, Black has doubled c-pawns and the half-open b-file; if not, the knight pressures the centre. It is playable but loosens the compact structure on which this defence rests.

Guards e5 and f6 and keeps the structure intact, but the knight shuts in the c8 bishop and costs time. White's knight jumps to f5, hitting the bishop on e7 and the d6 pawn, so Black has to trade or retreat the bishop on White's terms and stays cramped.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4 Bd7.name: Philidor Defence: Boden Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4 Bd7.strategy: Develops the bishop and covers c6 and e6, ready for ...Nc6 with a tempo on the queen. The cost is passivity: the bishop blocks Black's own queen and the knight on b8, so Black is a little behind in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4 Nc6.strategy: Develops with tempo: the knight attacks the queen, which has to move again. Black gets a natural development against a queen that came out early, and White's edge is no more than a little extra space.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight and blocks the queen's diagonal to g7, so the g7 pawn is safe whenever the bishop moves. The knight does not attack the queen, so White can finish development calmly, but Black is solid and ready to castle.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Bc4.strategy: Aims at the weakened king's side: with f7 empty after the pawn advance, a knight on g5 and a queen check on h5 become real threats. The most convincing way for White to get a clear advantage against the counter-gambit.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.dxe5.strategy: Takes on e5 and heads for a very sharp game: after ...fxe4 the knight has to move at once, and Black can rebuild the centre with ...d5. White still stands better, but the attack is slower and riskier than with the bishop on c4.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Nc3.name: Philidor Defence: Philidor Countergambit, Zukertort Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Nc3.background: Sometimes called the Zukertort Variation, after Johannes Zukertort.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 and sets a trap: if Black takes on e4 and plays the natural ...d5, the e5 pawn falls with a queen check on h5 and a raid on g6. But Black can recapture with ...Nf6 and avoid it, so White keeps only a lasting edge, well short of what the bishop attack wins.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Bc4 exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn instead of developing, and the lost time tells: White's knight jumps at once and the king's side is under heavy pressure. Black needed to bring a piece out, above all ...Nc6, to hold the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Bc4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and defends e5, so the centre holds before the weakened king's side is tested. White keeps an edge in a closed position with more space, but the game is slower than after taking on d4 and Black has time to bring the pieces out.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Bc4 Nf6.strategy: The knight jumps to g5 at once: f7 is a hole that the bishop already watches, and Black's natural replies lose either a piece (...d5 meets dxe5 and exf6) or the safety of the king.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Bc4 fxe4.strategy: Grabs the pawn but opens the king's side. After Nxe5 Black cannot recapture: ...dxe5 allows Qh5+ and Qxe5+, winning the rook on h8, and ...d5 runs into the same check on h5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Bc4 exd4 5.Ng.strategy: Aims the knight at f7, which is empty and covered by the bishop on c4, so Nf7 forking queen and rook is threatened. Black can parry with ...Nh6, and White has then moved the same knight twice before castling. Sound and sharp, but a step behind simple development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Bc4 exd4 5.O-.strategy: Develops and castles first, since Black has spent four moves on pawns: the pawn on d4 can be taken later. White gets a lead in development and a rook heading for the e-file against a king's side that is already loose.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Bc4 exd4 5.Nx.strategy: Recaptures the pawn at once and keeps the knight in the centre, where it eyes f5. It is sound, but it spends a tempo on material while Black's pieces are still at home, and White loses some of the force of an immediate attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Bc4 exd4 5.Ng.strategy: Parries the fork by guarding f7 and brings a piece out, though the knight on the rim is awkward. Black keeps the extra pawn for now but must finish development before White's pieces strike.

Guards f7 with the queen, but the bishop check on f7 drives the king to d8, where it loses castling and the queen is tied to the defence. White keeps the initiative against a king stuck in the centre.
Develops and ignores the threat: the knight jump to f7 forks queen and rook, and the king cannot take it because the bishop guards the square. Black loses the exchange for nothing.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Bc4 exd4 5.Ng.name: Philidor Defence: Lopez Countergambit, Jaenisch Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Bc4 exd4 5.Ng.background: Called the Jaenisch Variation, after Carl Jaenisch.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.Bc4 exd4 5.Ng.strategy: Wins a pawn and attacks the bishop on f8, but the knight is cut off from the rest of White's army and the rook on h8 can simply take it. White has to prove that the attack on the king's side makes up for the knight, whereas simply castling keeps a clearer advantage.

Castles and completes development, since Black's king is still in the centre and the knight on h6 is awkward. White lets Black keep the extra pawn for now in return for a lead in development and a lasting initiative.
Regains the pawn at once and eyes g7, but the queen comes out early and Black can develop with a tempo on it. It is sound, but White loses time and the initiative is less certain than after castling.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.dxe5 fxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn with a tempo on the knight, which must leave f3. Black has swapped a flank pawn for White's e-pawn, opens the f-file and aims to rebuild the centre with ...d5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.dxe5 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight and eyes e5 and d4 instead of taking on e4 at once. Black keeps the tension, but White can capture on d6 and stay a pawn up for the moment, so development has to make up for the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.dxe5 dxe5.strategy: Recaptures with the d-pawn but invites the queen swap: after Qxd8+ Kxd8 Black has lost castling, and the knight takes on e5 with a lead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.dxe5 fxe4 5.N.strategy: The knight steps aside with a threat on e4 and keeps the d-file open for the queen, instead of blocking it on d4 or d2. Black has to rebuild a centre at once while White has the more active pieces.

Retreats to attack e4, but the knight blocks the queen's file and the bishop on c1. Black rebuilds the centre with ...d5, or even gains a tempo with ...e3 against the knight, so White gives up the edge the pawn exchange should have brought.

Steps to d4 and keeps the queen's diagonal to h5 open, so the pawn grab ...dxe5? loses the rook to Qh5+. But Black simply rebuilds the centre with ...d5, and White has moved the same knight twice for a small edge.
Defends the e4 pawn and refills the centre. The price is a loose king's side: the e8-h5 diagonal and the e6 square are weak, so White strikes at once.
Takes the pawn back and offers the queen swap: after Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nxe4 White regains the pawn, Black's king is stuck in the centre without castling, and White has the more active pieces.
Develops and hits e5 but leaves the e4 pawn alone. White pins the knight with Bb5 and wins the pawn back, leaving Black a pawn down but with a playable game. Sound, though not the most resilient.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.dxe5 fxe4 5.N.name: Philidor Defence: Philidor Countergambit, del Rio Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.dxe5 fxe4 5.N.background: The del Rio Attack, named after Ercole del Rio, has been known since 1763.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 f5 4.dxe5 fxe4 5.N.strategy: The main move: the pawn cramps Black and supports a knight jump to f7 that would fork queen and rook, so Black has to react at once. The position is very sharp and favours White, because Black's pieces are loose.

Develops a piece and adds a second attacker to the e4 pawn, but lets go of the cramping advance. The pawn on e5 has no defender, so Black gets time to challenge it and develop, the initiative the knight jump created fades, and the edge is gone.

Hits the d5 pawn at once to break up Black's centre before it settles. Black gets a check and a counter-thrust that keep the game very sharp, but White's lead in development still gives the better chances; it is less direct than the cramping advance.

A rook sacrifice: Black ignores the knight jump to f7 and develops with threats along the diagonal to f2, hoping for activity. White simply takes the e4 pawn and keeps control, so the sacrifice does not pay off.

The most resilient answer: the check forces White to block before the knight can jump to f7, and the bishop stays active while Black keeps the e4 and d5 pawns as a base. White is still better developed and has the cramping pawn on e6, so the game stays very sharp.

Brings the knight out to guard f7, so the knight jump there loses its sting, and keeps the c8 bishop aimed at the e6 pawn. But the knight stands on the rim, White gets time to develop and hit e4, and Black has to defend carefully to keep material level.

Allows the knight jump to f7, which forks queen and rook, so Black gives up the exchange. In return the e6 pawn falls and the knight that takes the rook is stranded on h8, so Black gets a pawn, quick development and chances to trap it. Messy and risky.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4.strategy: The most testing reply: the bishop aims at f7 and revives the threat of taking on e5, because Black cannot recapture comfortably. Natural developing moves lose a pawn here, so Black has to know exactly how to answer.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Nc3.strategy: A quieter developing move that gives Black time to complete the set-up. White keeps the choice of plans and a small space edge but forgoes the pressure on f7.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.c4.strategy: Takes more space with the c-pawn, answering Black's passive set-up with a broad grip on the centre. Black's strongpoint on e5 stays intact and nothing in the position is weak, so White gains room but no concrete edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.dxe5.strategy: Resolves the tension at once, but it gets White little: after ...dxe5 the knight on d7 blocks the d-file, so there is no queen trade, and Black recaptures comfortably with a solid centre. White has given up the central tension without a gain.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 c6.strategy: Takes d5 away from White's queen, so recapturing on e5 no longer runs into Qd5, and opens a diagonal for Black's queen. It holds the centre, but White keeps the bishop pair and a lasting small edge, so it is a step behind resolving the centre at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 Nb6.name: Philidor Defence: Hanham Variation, Sharp Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 Nb6.strategy: Attacks the bishop at once, but the knight leaves d7 and gives up its guard of e5. The bishop retreats with a gain of time and the threat of taking on e5 returns, so Black has to give up the centre and White gets the better development and more space.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 exd4.strategy: Removes the e5 pawn from the line of fire, so the dxe5 tactics around f7 disappear and Black can develop freely. The price is the strongpoint on e5 and some space, and the bishop on c4 still eyes f7, so Black keeps a solid but slightly passive game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 c6 5.O-O.name: Philidor Defence: Hanham Variation, Krause Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 c6 5.O-O.strategy: Gets the king safe before opening the centre: the pawn exchange on e5 then works tactically against f7 and typically leaves White the bishop pair and a small plus. Black has to know the lines precisely.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 c6 5.Nc3.name: Philidor Defence: Hanham Variation, Schlechter Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 c6 5.Nc3.strategy: Natural development: it supports e4 and brings a piece out while keeping the central break in reserve. But it is less sharp than castling first and gives Black time to complete the set-up and castle, so White's edge is small.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 c6 5.c3.name: Philidor Defence: Hanham Variation, Delmar Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 c6 5.c3.strategy: Quieter than castling: the c-pawn backs up d4 for a broad pawn centre, but it takes c3 from the knight and removes the tactical bite of trading on e5. The game is calm, and White's edge, if any, is small.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 c6 5.Ng5.name: Philidor Defence: Hanham, Kmoch Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 c6 5.Ng5.strategy: Doubles the attack on f7, which only the king guards, but Black can simply defend it. The knight has then left the centre for little, and Black finishes development comfortably.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 c6 5.O-O.strategy: Completes the compact set-up: the d6 pawn and the d7 knight hold e5, and the bishop clears the way for castling. Black accepts a cramped position, with the c8 bishop shut in behind the knight, for a solid structure White has to work to undermine.

Resolves the central tension before White can use it, so there is no dxe5 trick to fear and Black develops freely. The price is the strongpoint on e5 and a little space, so Black gets a solid, slightly passive game.

Brings the second knight out, but the e5 pawn is now vulnerable: after dxe5, retaking with the pawn allows Ng5 with a double attack on f7, and retaking with the knight allows Bxf7+, so Black drops a pawn in the natural lines.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 c6 5.O-O.name: Philidor Defence: Hanham Variation, Steiner Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Bc4 c6 5.O-O.strategy: Resolves the central tension while Black's pieces are tangled, and each recapture has a catch. Taking with the knight loses the e5 pawn to Nxe5 and Qh5, which hits e5 and f7. Taking with the pawn allows Ng5, and White gets the bishop pair and kingside pressure.

Develops and supports e4, but lets the moment pass. Black's g8 knight and c8 bishop are still shut in, and after ...Ngf6 Black untangles and castles, so White gives up the quickest way to profit from the cramped set-up and the edge.

Puts the rook behind the e4 pawn and keeps the tension, a useful but slow move that develops no minor piece. Black is not forced to decide anything yet and can use the time to bring out the g8 knight, so White's pressure fades.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Nc3 Ngf6.strategy: Brings the second knight out against e4 while the d6 pawn and the d7 knight keep e5 guarded. With the bishop not yet on c4, nothing hits f7, so the development is safe. Black holds the centre in a solid but slightly passive set-up and waits for White to commit.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Nc3 exd4.strategy: Gives up the strongpoint on e5 that this set-up is built around. White recaptures with a knight in the centre and has more space, while the d7 knight keeps the c8 bishop shut in, so Black is solid but passive and has little to play for.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nd7 4.Nc3 c6.strategy: Takes d5 away from White's pieces and opens a diagonal for the queen, aiming at a compact set-up. But the g8 knight stays at home and e5 is held only by the d6 pawn and the d7 knight, so White's dxe5 ideas and pressure on f7 stay in the air.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move and makes the threat real again: if Black leaves e5 unguarded, a pawn trade and a queen trade win it. White keeps the tension and invites a slow, manoeuvring game in which Black must hold e5 with careful development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.dxe5.name: Philidor Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.dxe5.strategy: Cashes in the tension at once and takes the opening's calm out of it. Black has to win the pawn back on e4, because 4...dxe5 loses material to a queen trade and Nxe5. White keeps a slight lead in development and the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.Bc4.name: Philidor Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation, Klein Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop toward f7 and lets Black take on e4. After 4...Nxe4 5.dxe5, the natural recapture dxe5 and a queen trade leave Black's king in the centre with f7 under pressure, so Black needs the calmer 5...c6. Sound, but uncommon.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.Ng5.name: Philidor Defence: Nimzowitsch, Locock Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.Ng5.strategy: Defends e4 by moving the same knight twice and so gives Black the centre: ...exd4 and free development. Its hope is a trap: after ...h6 and dxe5, the natural ...dxe5? loses a rook to Qxd8+ Kxd8 Nxf7+. Sound enough, but it asks Black nothing.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.dxe5 Nxe4.strategy: Regains the pawn at once and keeps the queens on. It is the right recapture, since 4...dxe5 5.Qxd8+ Kxd8 6.Nxe5 loses material. The cost is an exposed knight on a central square, which White can attack with gain of time.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.dxe5 Ng4.strategy: Attacks e5 a second time and eyes f2, but the knight is loose on the rim: Bg5 attacks the queen with gain of time, and after the pawn exchange on d6 White is a pawn up with the better game. Black has lost a tempo for nothing.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.dxe5 Nfd7.strategy: Steps the attacked knight back, but loses a pawn: White takes on d6 and Black's retake leaves it a pawn down. The knight also blocks the c8 bishop and Black has lost a tempo, so White gets the better centre and the more active game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.dxe5 Nxe4 5..name: Philidor Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation, Rellstab Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.dxe5 Nxe4 5..strategy: Attacks the loose knight with the queen and forces it to move, keeping Black's undeveloped pieces under pressure. The queen is exposed in the centre, but it also stops Black defending the knight with ...d5. A queen trade often follows, leaving White a small, lasting lead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.dxe5 Nxe4 5..name: Philidor Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation, Sokolsky Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.dxe5 Nxe4 5..strategy: A quiet way to challenge the knight: it develops a piece and asks the knight to move or trade. Unlike the queen sortie it keeps no initiative, so Black can exchange knights and recapture on e5 to reach an easy, equal game.
Captures on d6, but Black simply retakes with ...Bxd6, a developing move: the active knight stays on e4 and the position is level. A natural move that gives White no edge.
